Elastic net by coordinate descent, with cross-validation

Source: R/learn.R
enpath.Rd

Fits the lasso, ridge and elastic net path by cyclical coordinate descent, for a numeric (gaussian) or a 0/1 (binomial) outcome, and cross-validates it over folds the caller supplies. The objective, the standardisation of the columns and the scale of lambda are those of 'glmnet', so that with the same lambda and the same folds the two give the same coefficients, up to their convergence thresholds: the gaussian family minimises (1 / 2n) |y - a0 - x b|^2 + lambda pen(b), the binomial family the mean negative log-likelihood plus lambda pen(b), with pen(b) = sum((1 - alpha) / 2 (s b)^2 + alpha |s b|), s the population standard deviations of the columns. For the gaussian family the outcome is scaled to unit variance while fitting, as 'glmnet' does. The intercept is never penalised; a constant column keeps a zero coefficient.

Usage

enpath(
  x,
  y,
  fam = "gaussian",
  alpha = 1,
  lambda = NULL,
  nlam = 100,
  lmr = NULL,
  fold = NULL,
  tol = 1e-07,
  maxit = 1e+05,
  scr = TRUE
)

Arguments

x

The predictors: a numeric matrix, one row per observation, with no missing values.

y

The outcome: one finite number per row of x; 0 or 1 for the binomial family.

fam

"gaussian" or "binomial".

alpha

The mixing parameter, from 0 (ridge) to 1 (lasso).

lambda

NULL, or the penalties to fit: non-negative numbers in decreasing order.

nlam

When lambda is NULL, the number of penalties on the path: one whole number, at least 1.

lmr

When lambda is NULL, the smallest penalty as a share of the largest: one number strictly between 0 and 1, or NULL for 1e-4 when x has more rows than columns and 0.01 otherwise. The path runs from the smallest penalty that zeroes every coefficient down to lmr times it, evenly spaced on the log scale, and stops early as 'glmnet' does: from the fifth penalty on, once the share of the deviance explained grows by less than 1e-5 of itself or exceeds 0.999.

fold

NULL, or the fold of each row: whole numbers from 1 to the number of folds (at least 2), each fold used.

tol

The convergence threshold: a pass that moves no standardised coefficient by more than sqrt(tol) (weighted by the curvature, for the binomial family) ends the descent. One positive number.

maxit

The most passes over the columns, in all: one whole number.

scr

TRUE to screen the columns of a binomial path by the sequential strong rule of Tibshirani et al. (2012) before each penalty (faster; the optimality conditions are still checked over every column, so the solution does not change), FALSE to cycle over the active columns only. Ignored for the gaussian family.

Value

A list: lambda, the penalties fitted; a0, the intercepts; beta, a matrix of coefficients with one column per penalty and one row per column of x; and, when fold is given, cvm and cvsd, the mean held-out loss (squared error, or the binomial deviance with probabilities kept within 1e-5 of 0 and 1) and its standard error over folds, computed as 'glmnet' computes them, lmin, the penalty at the minimum, and l1se, the largest penalty within one standard error of it; these four are NULL without folds.

Details

Speed against accuracy: tol and maxit set how far the descent goes. The default tol = 1e-7 is glmnet's; tol = 1e-20, maxit = 1e7 is the exact setting, which reproduces glmnet run at the same threshold to 1e-8 in every coefficient (tests). Between the two, the penalised objective at each penalty differs by less than 1e-6 of its value (tested on the gaussian and binomial paths). nlam and lmr set the length and the end of a path chosen here, and scr the screening of a binomial path.

Each coordinate step is the minimiser of its one-dimensional objective, by soft-thresholding, the proximal map of the absolute value: see proof("enpath").

The binomial fit is a proximal Newton method: iteratively reweighted least squares around coordinate descent over the active columns, with the optimality conditions checked over every column before a lambda is left. The gaussian fit updates the gradient through the column inner products, formed only for the columns that enter the model.

References

Friedman, J., Hastie, T. and Tibshirani, R. (2010). Regularization paths for generalized linear models via coordinate descent. Journal of Statistical Software, 33(1), 1-22. doi:10.18637/jss.v033.i01

Tibshirani, R., Bien, J., Friedman, J., Hastie, T., Simon, N., Taylor, J. and Tibshirani, R. J. (2012). Strong rules for discarding predictors in lasso-type problems. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 74(2), 245-266. doi:10.1111/j.1467-9868.2011.01004.x

Examples

set.seed(1)
x <- matrix(rnorm(200 * 5), 200)
y <- x[, 1] - 0.5 * x[, 2] + rnorm(200)
f <- enpath(x, y, nlam = 20, fold = rep(1:5, 40))
f$lmin
#> [1] 0.04707722
f$beta[, f$lambda == f$lmin]
#> [1]  0.8700394 -0.4704137  0.0000000  0.0000000 -0.0208658
